entry.title: The Fishbowl — your memory lives here, you don't
entry.summary: A self-hosted home for notes, calendar, contacts, mail and files: every workspace a folder of its own, search that finds what you mean on your own CPU, and an MCP server that lets an agent work in it without letting it loose.
entry.content:
The Fishbowl is where my notes, todos, calendar, contacts, mail and files live. It runs on my own machine, it is open source, and an AI agent can work in it — remember things, find them, sort the mail, build a small app for a shared space — without getting more than I hand it. I started it in April, v0.6.0 is out, and the repository is public.

Why

Tools like this exist, and the pattern is familiar: free to start, useful enough to depend on, and then exports get harder and features move behind a price. The Fishbowl starts from the other end. A tool that earns its keep doesn't need to hold your data to keep you, so leaving has to cost nothing.

  • Every workspace is a folder. My personal one and every shared space is one SQLite database with its files beside it, in a folder of its own. Stop the host and that folder is the whole workspace; while it runs, export hands out the same as a ZIP, any time, without asking.
  • Files stay files. What goes into Files lies on disk under its real name, in a real folder tree, not as blobs in a table.
  • Nothing phones home. The interface loads nothing from anyone else's servers. What talks to the outside world is what I set up: my mail servers, Discord, a Google sign-in if I want one — and, once, the download of the search model.

What is in the bowl

One desktop in the browser, built on SACRVM APPKIT: tiles that show what is in them — the next dates, open todos, unread mail — and a command palette (Ctrl/⌘K) that searches everything as you type.

  • Notes in markdown, with :::secret blocks encrypted in the browser. The key opens with a passphrase, 24 recovery words or a passkey; the server only ever stores ciphertext, and neither search nor an agent sees what is inside.
  • Calendar with full recurrence rules, .ics import and export, subscription links for the phone, and the contacts' birthdays.
  • Contacts: people and organisations, vCard and CSV both ways, duplicates found and merged.
  • Mail from iCloud, Gmail, IONOS or any IMAP server, every account in one list. The Fishbowl keeps its own copy and uses IMAP only as the transport, so search, tags and rules work across accounts. New mail arrives by push, and writing is markdown. Spam is read live from the server and never stored, so it never reaches search or an agent.
  • Files: a two-pane commander, made for the keyboard.
  • Todos, in the order I drag them.

And the conversation: a Discord bot to remember something, search, see what is coming, get reminders and a short morning digest. It answers with titles only; the content stays in the bowl.

Finding by meaning

Search blends two rankings: the words, from SQLite's full-text index, and the meaning, from multilingual-e5-small. That small model runs on the machine's own CPU and turns every note, mail and searchable table row into a vector. "That thing about the venue last month" finds the note even when it used other words. German works as well as English, which the first, English-only model never managed. A hit with all the words still comes first: a name means little to a model.

Spaces

A space is a workspace shared with others: the family, a club, a team. Roles go from Reader to Owner, and invitations are links. Each space is its own folder again, with its own notes, calendar, mail and files, plus tables.

Tables are a small database the space defines for itself: typed columns, and links that work like foreign keys, so nothing that is linked to can be deleted. On top of them a space can have its own apps: plain JavaScript files in the space's .apps folder, run in a sandboxed frame, with the space's data handed in through one object. A table can have triggers, small scripts in a JavaScript sandbox that check or change a row before it is written.

Built for agents

The Fishbowl is an MCP server: 40 tools over notes, contacts, the calendar, mail, files, tables and a space's apps. The calendar is read-only on purpose: an agent scheduling your days has sharper consequences than one remembering a note. Claude Code connects with one command:

claude mcp add --transport http fishbowl https://<your-host>/mcp \
  --header "Authorization: Bearer <key>"

On a public HTTPS host, claude.ai connects as a custom connector with OAuth instead. Either way the same rules hold:

  • A key is one workspace and a list of scopes: read notes, write contacts, read mail. Sending mail is a scope of its own and part of no default level, because a key that can read mail and send it could be steered by a crafted mail. On every request a key is cut down to what its owner may still do in that space.
  • What an agent writes waits for review. A note from an agent carries review:pending until a person edits it.
  • Secrets never cross the wire, and mail reaches an agent marked as untrusted: data from its sender, never an instruction.
  • An agent can build an app for a space. space_guide writes it the space's tables, apps, house rules and latest errors as one page of markdown; the file tools write the code; app_errors tells it what broke when someone opened it.

The agents find the gaps, too. On 29 October one asked which account it should send a mail from instead of guessing. The tool took only an internal id and fell back to the first account, so that was the tool's fault, not the agent's. Now an agent names the address, and in a workspace with several accounts Fishbowl refuses to pick one for it.

How it is made

.NET 10 and ASP.NET Core on the server; SQLite through Dapper, with sqlite-vec for the vectors; MailKit for mail and Ical.Net for calendars. The interface is vanilla JavaScript without a build step, on SACRVM APPKIT, with sac-md-editor for notes and sac-data-grid for tables, in English and German. It ships as one self-contained binary for Windows, Linux and macOS and runs under Husky, which supervises it and installs updates from GitHub Releases. It fetches its own HTTPS certificate. About 1,300 tests keep it honest, 154 of them in a real browser. The licence is AGPL-3.0.

Where it stands

v0.6.0 came out on 2 November, and it is the release with everything above: mail, the multilingual search, the full calendar and the space apps arrived after v0.5.0. It is early, and kept small on purpose: external sync, a scripting layer and a plugin ecosystem were planned and dropped rather than half-built.

Questions: mail@sacrvm.dev.

entry.title: Voxcade — an arcade engine made of little cubes
entry.summary: A voxel arcade engine in Rust, two weeks old: destructible worlds that fill the screen, games written in Lua, and built from the first commit so an AI agent can help write them.
entry.content:
Voxcade is a voxel arcade engine. Everything is made of little cubes, everything can be blown apart, and it has to feel like an arcade machine. The plan: the classic 2D genres, rebuilt in voxels — with an AI agent at your side that can see, test and change what you build. It is two weeks old, the repository is still private and there is nothing to download yet — but there is enough to tell.

Where it comes from

Voxatron proved the idea: a whole world of destructible voxels, small games, instant fun. It never left alpha and is no longer developed. Voxcade keeps the idea and the feel, not the implementation, and changes three things:

  • The world fills the screen instead of floating in a box.
  • The GPU does the drawing. Rust and wgpu, on Vulkan, Metal or DirectX 12; SDL3 for the window, gamepads and sound.
  • Open formats, own editors. Models are MagicaVoxel .vox files and levels are plain JSON, so the voxel editor you already use works. The IDE brings its own voxel and level editors as well, and Tiled maps come in with one import.

The look

One fixed camera per game, in perspective, that only moves across the ground. A top-down RPG, a 2.5D jump & run and an arena shooter are just different angles. The figures are small and plain — 10 to 20 voxels tall, one colour per material, every voxel deliberate: the 8-bit charm in clean cubes. The engine does the light and the shade, sun shadows included, and a model can be lit voxel by voxel like pixel art, so a round shape shades softly and only its outline stays blocky.

And things break the way they look. After a blast the debris settles back into the world, and whatever no longer connects to the ground falls.

A game is a folder

After LÖVE: conf.lua sets the game up, main.lua is the game.

function on_level_start(how)              -- the level begins
  level:fill(0, 0, 0, 127, 127, 0, "#3b4150")   -- a floor
  level.state.keeper = level:spawn("keeper", 64, 64)
  level.camera:look_at(64, 64)
end

function on_tick()                        -- 60 times a second
  local keeper = level.state.keeper
  keeper:walk(input.dir, 40)
  if input:pressed("jump") then keeper:jump(8) end
end

Every length is in voxels, every speed in voxels per second. Whoever prefers Rust uses the engine as a library instead.

Built for agents

The goal from the first commit: anyone should be able to write a great game with it, and an AI agent should be able to help. That shaped the engine as much as the cubes did.

  • Everything is text. Rules in Lua, settings in conf.lua, models as .vox, levels as JSON, music as MML, sound effects as a few numbers each. People, agents and editors work on the same files, and the game plays a change the moment it is saved.
  • The API documents itself. It ships as a Lua definition file with LuaLS annotations, so editors and agents get completion and checks from the same source, and voxcade api prints any part of it.
  • Seeing without a window. voxcade shot plays a game with scripted input and saves one frame; the same command always gives the same picture. That is how an agent sees what it built. voxcade inspect prints how the game stands as JSON, and voxcade film turns a run into an MP4 or GIF.
  • Checking without playing. The simulation is deterministic: seeded random numbers, maths that is bit-identical on Linux, Windows and macOS, and all game state in plain tables that are hashed every tick. So a replay is a test and a bug report at once, and voxcade check plays every one and says whether it still runs as recorded. The same replays run on the title screen in attract mode, as an arcade machine would.
  • One MCP server. voxcade mcp hands an agent the frame, the game's state, the checks and the API as tools, and claude mcp add voxcade -- voxcade mcp is the whole setup in Claude Code.

The IDE goes one step further. Logic and assets on the left, one editor in the middle, voxel and level editors beside it, PLAY and BUILD — and a console with Claude Code in it, one conversation per game. Through the IDE's own MCP tools the agent sees what you see: the open file and the cursor, errors down to file, line and tick, the running frame. It can act too: show you a file at a line, start the game and stop it. It edits through the files, and the IDE takes its changes in.

What plays today

A handful of small games already run on it, each in a different genre — shooters, a jump & run, a puzzle game, a farming sim — and each there to prove a part of the engine. One of them is written in Rust instead of Lua, to show that the second way in works too.

Sound and music are synthesized: a SID-like synth, and songs written in MML, a music notation an agent can write as well as a person.

Voxcade is a prototype, and the repository stays private while it grows. When there is something to play, it will be here. Questions until then: mail@sacrvm.dev.

Insert coin.

entry.title: Hello, CachyOS — new machine, new OS, one move
entry.summary: Why I left Windows for CachyOS: a laptop screen I could barely use, a desktop I wanted anyway, and the wish to own my system again — swapped in one go.
entry.content:
Two days ago this site moved house. Not the server — GitHub Pages still serves it — but the machine it is written on. The Windows laptop is retired, a new AMD desktop runs CachyOS, and this is the first entry written on it.

Why leave

The short answer: control over my own system. The long answer has a switch in it.

My laptop is an ASUS gaming machine — sinfully expensive, once. It pairs an Intel iGPU with an NVIDIA card and a MUX chip, the piece of hardware that decides which of the two drives the built-in display. Windows and that wretched MUX stopped getting along, to the point where I could barely use the laptop's own screen. A machine you have to work around is not quite your machine anymore.

Linux has a fix for that MUX, down at the kernel level. But Intel plus NVIDIA on Linux is a chapter of its own, I wanted a desktop again anyway, and hardware prices were only going one way. So the computer and the operating system changed in one move.

The machine

  • AMD all the way. Ryzen 9 9900X, Radeon RX 9070 XT, 32 GB of RAM. The graphics driver ships with the kernel and Mesa — nothing to download, nothing to install separately.
  • CachyOS. Arch underneath, with its own tuned kernel, an LTS kernel next to it as the fallback, and package repositories built specifically for Zen 4 and Zen 5 CPUs.
  • KDE Plasma on Wayland. The desktop closest to what a Windows user already knows.
  • btrfs with Snapper. Every package transaction leaves a snapshot behind, and the Limine boot menu lists them. A bad update is a reboot away from undone.

Games

Steam runs with CachyOS's own Proton build; Lutris and Heroic cover everything outside Steam, with Wine underneath. Cyberpunk 2077 and Onimusha: Way of the Sword are the first two on the drive.

Work

  • .NET runs natively — SDK, runtime, the lot. Most of what I build is .NET or vanilla JavaScript, and both are at home here.
  • VS Code, git and the GitHub CLI, the same tools as before.
  • fish as the shell.
  • The repositories moved from D:\repos to ~/Projects/repos.

The rough edges

Not everything is smooth. The UI is fiddly now and then. Discord wants a different launcher — here it is Vesktop. Some things don't run on the first try.

None of it was big. And this is where the old line "Linux is for people who enjoy fixing Linux" stops being true: with Claude in the terminal, an error message becomes a conversation, and a Linux is tamed in no time.

Questions, or your own switch story: mail@sacrvm.dev.

Mine again.

entry.title: SACRVM APPKIT — the kit, a desktop, and two apps to prove it
entry.summary: A zero-dependency HTML UI kit — forty-one web components, one-variable theming, install-by-URL apps — with a live desktop at desktop.sacrvm.dev to try in the browser.
entry.content:
SACRVM APPKIT is a UI kit for the web with no build step: some forty sac-* web components, a theming engine that derives every colour from one --accent variable, and an app system that installs apps by URL. You vendor one folder of plain files, link one stylesheet and one script, and write HTML. No framework, no bundler, no node_modules — F5 is the toolchain.

Try it before reading on

The proof runs at desktop.sacrvm.dev: a desktop in your browser. It is a host, not an app — it owns the home screen and the bare stage, and every app on it is installed by URL from somebody else's repository. Reading a manifest and running code are two separate steps: the desktop shows what it found, names the origin on every tile, and asks before anything executes. The app list lives in your browser's localStorage — no server, no account.

On your first visit the desktop offers its two reference apps, so the stage does not start empty:

  • Calculator — a window app: one custom element, one classic script, and a proper two-register pocket-calculator brain in ~400 dependency-free lines.
  • Notes — a view app: it draws its own chrome, the note list is the rail, and every note gets its own link.

Their repos are worked examples — see it done properly. To start your own app, don't strip a calculator down to a skeleton; there is a starting point built for the job. Zero to running on the desktop is three steps:

  1. Use this template on sacrvm-app-template — a clean repo with the right shape from commit one: app.json, app.js, app.css, a vendored kit/. Rename five strings.
  2. Enable GitHub Pages — now your app has a URL.
  3. Hand out the link — https://desktop.sacrvm.dev/?install=<your-pages-url> runs the ordinary confirm flow, and your app is on the desktop.

The kit itself

  • Two files. kit/css/ui.css carries the design tokens and the global stylesheet, kit/js/all.js carries every component. The kit/ folder is vendored verbatim; kit/VERSION says which release you hold.
  • The components. Floating draggable windows, a nav ribbon with burger panel, sidebar and split workspace layouts, dialogs, menus, toasts, tooltips, tabs — and form controls down to a colour picker and a date field.
  • Seed-derived theming. Light, dark and auto via data-theme; every colour is color-mix()-derived from one --accent. An app re-themes from a single variable, at runtime, with no build.
  • A runtime, not just widgets. window.sac.* brings the router, the dialog and toast services, a Ctrl-K command palette, sandboxed storage, and sac.apps — the install-by-URL system the desktop is built on.
  • Scaffolds included. kit/templates/ ships complete app skeletons and page-level scaffolds — the folder of plain files contains its own starting points.

No build step, on purpose

Vendoring is the whole upgrade story: delete kit/, unzip the new release, F5. The kit ships as a ZIP of plain files from GitHub Releases, MIT licensed. Nothing is transpiled, nothing is locked — what you commit is what runs.

The style guide with every token and component lives in the appkit repo; the desktop's long-form "How this works" is at desktop.sacrvm.dev/how.html. Feedback and bug reports to the issue tracker or mail@sacrvm.dev.

F5 is the toolchain.

entry.title: JUST PLAY 0.6.0 beta — The Library
entry.summary: JUST TAG ships — multi-file tag editing, pattern renaming, previewed file operations. Plus the indexed Pre-Cue Finder and one shared track table.
entry.content:
JUST PLAY is the music player for DJs and music lovers. Drop tracks in, double-click to play. Camelot key, BPM and energy detected on the spot — no library to build, no sign-in, no nag.

JUST TAG ships

The tag editor is packaged, installed and on the Start menu for the first time. It browses the disk, not a library — the tool for a download that just landed somewhere no index has seen.

  • Multi-file editing, a tick per field. Fields the selection disagrees on say different values, so nothing is flattened by accident.
  • %artist% - %title% builds a file name from tags, or reads tags out of a name. Both directions, one language.
  • Move, copy and delete, every one previewed. There is no overwrite, ever — a taken name is a collision, and the answer is "leave both alone" or "keep both".
  • Search that reads as a sentence: sixteen fields, seven comparisons, including is empty. "Genre is empty" is the one that finds the damage.

Also in 0.6

  • The Pre-Cue Finder gained the index. Folders paint instantly and verify behind you, and you can filter across every playlist below a folder.
  • One track table across queue, finder and JUST TAG — same rows, same widths, sized to what is actually in them.
  • JUST STREAM shows the listener count, with no admin password stored.

Still pre-1.0

What is not done, said up front:

  • Nothing watches your library folder yet. The index catches up when you press Scan.
  • A scan indexes, it does not analyse. Use right-click Analyse, or the CLI.
  • macOS and Linux share the codebase and are not validated.

One installer, four tools, one shared runtime: JUST PLAY, JUST STREAM, JUST TAG and the headless CLI. Per-user, no admin prompt.

Download 0.6.0-beta.1 — feedback and bug reports to info@sacrvm.dev or the issue tracker.

From DJs to DJs.
